findings.claim: One Barossa house has kept a workshop inside its winery since the 1940s
findings.because: The answer (barrels, at Yalumba) is right, but the date in the stem is wrong. Yalumba's cooperage has worked on site since about the turn of the 20th century, with coopers there from around 1890. Yalumba describes it as more than a century old, with an early history that is not recorded. It did not start in the 1940s. The error is in the stem, not in an option.
sources: https://www.yalumba.com/the-cooperage/ (search snippet; the page itself did not load)
findings.fix: Replace 'since the 1940s' with 'for more than a century' (or 'since around the turn of the twentieth century').
findings.verifyReason: Confirmed. The stem says the workshop has been there "since the 1940s", which points to a founding date in that decade. Yalumba's own cooperage page (seen as a search snippet, because the page itself failed with too many redirects), The Louise and the Barossa tourism listings all say the cooperage's beginnings are unknown. They say coopers have worked there since about 1890, that coopering has been a tradition at Yalumba for more than a century, and that the cooperage has operated since about the turn of the 20th century. The coopers only moved into the current building ("The Cooperage") in the 1990s. None of these sources ties the cooperage to the 1940s. Read literally, "since the 1940s" is not strictly false, because a workshop open since about 1890 was also open in the 1940s. But the stem uses the date to identify the house, so a candidate would learn a wrong founding date. The keyed answer (oak barrels, at Yalumba) and the explanation are correct.
verifySources: https://www.yalumba.com/the-cooperage/ (search snippet only; the page failed with too many redirects)
findings.finalFix: In the stem, replace "has kept a workshop inside its winery since the 1940s" with "has kept a workshop inside its winery for more than a century". The rest of the question, the answer and the explanation stay as they are.

question.q: One Barossa house has kept a workshop inside its winery since the 1940s, turning out something almost every other winery in the world buys in. What does it make there?
accept: it makes its own oak barrels
it makes its own oak casks
it makes its own wooden barrels
it makes its own wooden casks
it makes its own wine barrels
it makes all its own barrels
it still makes its own barrels
it still makes its own oak barrels
oak barrels in its own cooperage
question.exp: Yalumba is the house, and a working cooperage lets it buy standing timber, season the staves for as long as it likes and build to its own specification rather than take what a supplier offers. Almost nobody else bothers, because the craft takes a cooper's whole working life to learn and one winery needs only a few hundred barrels a year.

findings.claim: The stem calls Cheval des Andes's Bordeaux partner (Château Cheval Blanc) "a Saint-Emilion first growth". Cheval Blanc no longer holds any Saint-Emilion rank.
findings.because: Cheval Blanc was Premier Grand Cru Classé A from 1955 through the 2012 classification. It withdrew and is not in the 2022 classification. Pavie and Figeac are now the only Premier Grand Cru Classé A estates, and Ausone and Angélus withdrew too. Calling Cheval Blanc a Saint-Emilion first growth stopped being true with the 2022 classification. The answer, Cheval des Andes, still stands.
findings.fix: A Saint-Emilion estate ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A until it left the classification in 2022 shares, with a Mendoza estate, a Malbec-led red grown on stony Andean ground at around a thousand metres. Name that wine.
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. Château Cheval Blanc, the Bordeaux partner in Cheval des Andes (confirmed on chevaldesandes.com, which also gives Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot), was Premier Grand Cru Classé A through the 2012 classification. It withdrew in 2021 and does not appear in the 2022 Saint-Emilion classification. Pavie and Figeac (promoted in 2022) are now the only "A" estates. Calling Cheval Blanc a Saint-Emilion first growth is therefore out of date since the 2022 classification. The answer, Cheval des Andes, and the accept list are still correct. The examiner's fix is slightly inaccurate on dates: Cheval Blanc announced its withdrawal in 2021 and was absent from the 2022 list. It did not "leave in 2022". It is better to phrase this as "stayed out of the 2022 classification". I could not open the legal text of the 2022 classification because the web search budget was used up. The ruling rests on the pages cited below.
findings.finalFix: A Saint-Emilion estate that was Premier Grand Cru Classé A until it stayed out of the 2022 classification shares, with a Mendoza estate, a Malbec-led red grown on stony Andean ground at around a thousand metres. Name that wine.

question.q: A Saint-Emilion first growth and a Mendoza estate share a Malbec-led red grown on stony Andean ground at around a thousand metres. Name that wine.
accept: the cheval des andes joint venture
question.exp: Malbec leads it and Cabernet Sauvignon fills it out, which is the Bordeaux partner's contribution to a grape Argentina had long bottled on its own. Mendoza's old ungrafted Malbec is the material such ventures are really after, since cuttings of that quality no longer exist in the variety's homeland.
